implementation_notes: The metadata store is the attribute set on the entity ([Table("users")], [Column("user_name")], [Key], [DatabaseGenerated], [NotMapped], [MaxLength]); the reader is EF Core's model builder, which merges annotations, conventions and explicit configuration into the EntityType metadata behind the DbContext, and the engine is the LINQ provider and update pipeline that persist and materialise entities from it. The per-class mapper disappears and a mapping change becomes an attribute edit. Prefer the Fluent API when the mapping must not live in the classes, when entities are shared with other layers, or when it needs forms attributes cannot express (owned types, value converters, composite keys).
pitfalls: Conventions fill every gap silently: a renamed property changes the column unless it was mapped explicitly or the model is validated against the schema at startup.
Attributes and Fluent API configuration can coexist and the Fluent API wins, so the effective mapping is not where a reader looks first.
Type/column mismatches are provider-level: a [Column(TypeName = ...)] that disagrees with the database fails on first materialisation, not at compile time.

variants.name: Fluent API / IEntityTypeConfiguration<T>
variants.implementation_notes: Instead of decorating the class, the mapping is declared in a separate IEntityTypeConfiguration<T> class (or in OnModelCreating) as method calls: ToTable("users"), Property(u => u.Name).HasColumnName("user_name").HasMaxLength(64), HasKey, Ignore and so on. The metadata store is code that runs once while the model is built, which keeps entities free of persistence attributes and can express mapping forms attributes cannot. Use it when entities are shared with other layers or when the mapping needs value converters, owned types and composite keys; the price is that the mapping is no longer readable from the class.
pitfalls: Configuration classes must be discovered: one that is not applied by ApplyConfigurationsFromAssembly is silently ignored and conventions decide the mapping.
Mapping that lives away from the class survives renames by compiling and failing only at query time.
